summary.text:
Read on Appendix C — the 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy — taken to the Governance and Audit Committee on 3 February 2026. The covering report is not in what we hold, so there is no contact officer block; the appendix itself names no officer and gives no address. All figures below are quoted from the appendix.

Position at 31 December 2025 (§3.1, Appendix 2): £75.7m of borrowing, all PWLB, weighted 5.49%; £130.7m of investments (£39m UK Government, £41m MMFs, £36.5m other local authorities, £13m pooled funds, £1.2m unsecured bank), weighted 4.13%. Net investor of £53.4m. Add £1.6m of lease liabilities and gross external debt is £77.3m.

The story in the paper's own tables is a controlled cash-down. Balance sheet resources fall from £232.8m at 31.3.25 to £149.8m at 31.3.26 (a single-year drop of £83m) and on to £126.9m by 31.3.27 — £106m over four years. Treasury investments consequently fall from £153.0m to £41.4m in one year and to £10.5m by 31.3.27. Internal borrowing rises from 46% of Loans CFR to 63%. The liability benchmark swings £115.8m over two years, from −£31.4m (net investor) at 31.3.25 to +£84.4m (net borrower) at 31.3.27, sitting £15.0m above current committed external borrowing at that date. §2.4 says no new long-term loans in 2026/27 and §5.3 tells you why: short-term is expected to be cheaper for the medium term. The paper is consistent — the £15m LB gap sits inside the 25% under-12-months limit — but the runway ends when the reserve drawdown stops.

The balance sheet identity ties at every year within £0.1m rounding (exact at 31.3.29). The LB identity is exact at every year.

The PWLB loan-book reconciliation fails at the paper's reference date: our file at 31.12.2025 shows 3 loans totalling £7,069,167, against the paper's £75.7m at 5.49%. This is a Start-date issue on our side (18 of our 21 live loans have Start dates after 31.12.2025, which cannot be right when the paper confirms £75.7m was already in place). Our aggregate at 31.3.2026 — 21 loans, £73.1m, weighted 5.65% — sits within £0.8m of Table 1's external borrowing estimate for 31.3.26 (£73.9m), so the shape ties even where the snapshot does not. Per EMAIL_TEMPLATE.md §7 the loan-book claim is left out of the email; the gap is recorded here.

Arlingclose's December 2025 central case (Appendix 1) is dated and testable: Bank Rate to 3.25% by mid-2026, 10-year gilt at 4.30% by September 2026. On 14 August 2026, Bank Rate is still 3.75% and PWLB Certainty 10y is 5.83% (implying a 10y gilt around 5.03%) — running 73bp above the central case for the current quarter. Not a criticism of the forecast; the frame is worth flagging back to them.

Two smaller finds: the pooled-fund yield budget of 3.7% (§10.1) sits about 2 points below the actual 5.69% at 31.12.25, worth roughly £259k a year of conservatism on £13m; the debt-interest budget of 5.7% sits 21bp above the current 5.49% weighted rate. Neither is a red flag.

Email drafted using the reserves-runoff story and the Arlingclose forecast as the two anchors — no loan-book reconciliation is asserted. It cannot ship until an officer name and address are added.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on Appendix C, the 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy that went to Governance and Audit on 3 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

The thing that stood out most is the shape of the balance sheet forecast in your Table 1. Balance sheet resources fall from £232.8m at 31 March 2025 to £149.8m at 31 March 2026 — an £83m single-year drop — and on to £126.9m by 31 March 2027. That £106m fall over four years is what allows treasury investments to run from £153.0m to £41.4m in the first year and to £10.5m by 31.3.27, and it is what your internal borrowing (rising from 46% of Loans CFR to 63%) is spending down. Your paragraph 2.4 says the Council will not need any new long-term loans in 2026/27, and your paragraph 5.3 says short-term will be cheaper anyway. Both consistent with the tables. The bit that reads across all of them is Table 2: the liability benchmark swings from −£31.4m at 31.3.25 (net investor by that measure) to +£84.4m at 31.3.27, a £115.8m shift in two years. At the peak the benchmark sits £15.0m above your committed external borrowing at that date — well inside the 25% under-12-months limit at §7.4, so bridgeable — but that is where the runway ends.

On Arlingclose's December central case (Appendix 1): Bank Rate to 3.25% by mid-2026 and the 10-year gilt at 4.30% by September. Six months on, Bank Rate is still 3.75% and PWLB Certainty 10y is 5.83% at today's PM fixing, notice 314/26 — which implies the 10y gilt is running near 5.03%. So the current-quarter central case is out by around 50bp on Bank Rate and 73bp on the 10-year. Not a criticism of the forecast; the point is that the £15m short-term bridge in the LB is being priced into a market that has moved more than the strategy assumed when it was written. Our daily curve, sector activity and the SONIA path are at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity if it helps in the next update.

And a smaller one that we noticed and thought worth flagging back. Your paragraph 10.1 budgets pooled-fund returns at 3.7% while your Appendix 2 shows the same £13m of pooled funds returning 5.69% at 31 December — about £259k a year of conservatism. Not a red flag, just visible when you set both lines next to each other.

A note on scope: we hold PWLB only — no LOBOs, no market debt, no bank loans — so any view we offer sits alongside your total borrowing rather than describing all of it. Your PWLB book, priced daily on the DMO's own formula, is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. That page is indicative and we say so plainly; the DMO's quote is the only one that binds, and we don't model MRP or accounting treatment, both of which would matter to any restructuring conversation.

All of the above sits underneath something CIPFA is putting in front of everyone: the liability benchmark as a mandatory prudential indicator, with updated Prudential and Treasury Codes on the way. Yours is already built and already talking — it is what most of this note reads off — which is the point. If members are getting to grips with it, Liability benchmark — building and using it and Internal borrowing and the cost of carry are two of the courses on our academy that sit against the tables above, and Treasury management for councillors and PWLB rates — reading the daily curve are the two written for the committee room. The academy is at pwlbtoday.org/academy, free to local authorities until the end of September, with free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find any of it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Appendix C — Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27, Governance and Audit Committee, 3 February 2026, https://democracy.gwynedd.llyw.cymru/documents/s48045/appendix-c-treasury-management-strategy.pdf.
